title: Secrets and Sensitive Information knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Secrets and Sensitive Information”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Avoiding hard-coded credentials” under lesson 134, “Secrets and Sensitive Information”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Secrets and Sensitive Information”?
options: Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
questions.answer_key: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.explanation: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Secrets and Sensitive Information”?
options: Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
questions.answer_key: Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials.
questions.explanation: Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
